periods.activity_title: Opening the Play: Guests, Manners and Mary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading pair discussion (p.70): Athithi Devo Bhava and guest etiquette.
Let us read — select polite behaviours from list (p.70): five-statement choice activity.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the play's title and genre (humorous dialogue) and invites students to name one rule of polite conversation they know. A quick paired exchange on the phrase 'Athithi Devo Bhava' and why guests deserve courtesy opens the discussion.

Teacher reads Scene I aloud while students follow in their textbooks (p.70–74), pausing to mark stage directions and character names. Students track how Mrs. Shaw coaches Mary as the reading proceeds.
Class works on 'Let us read' — choosing which of the five listed behaviours display politeness toward guests (p.70). Pairs discuss each option aloud before the class reaches a shared verdict.
Teacher draws out observations: which choices were obvious, which needed reasoning, and why criticising a guest's habits is on the list. Students note one insight in their exercise books.

periods.teacher_notes: Mrs. Shaw's coaching of Mary in Scene I establishes the comedy's engine — every rule she states will be broken in Scene II. Watch for students who conflate 'polite' with 'silent'; the play insists conversation must flow, not simply be inoffensive. A task left for self-study: the group discussion on handling rude classmates (p.70) — students may attempt it independently.

periods.activity_title: Scene I Close-Up: What Mrs. Shaw Really Means

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — complete Scene I table: speaker, words, reason (p.74).
Let us discuss — predict: will Mary follow advice successfully? (p.74).

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the coaching exchange between Mrs. Shaw and Mary in Scene I — the key rules about kindness, keeping conversation going, and the farewell phrase 'Must you go? Can't you stay?' — to anchor the guided work that follows.

Students work in pairs to complete the 'Let us discuss' table (p.74): Speaker | Words | Reason. Teacher circulates, prompting students to explain not just what Mary says but why Mrs. Shaw responds as she does. Pairs share one row each until the table is complete.

Class takes up the prediction question: will Mary manage to follow her mother's advice when the guests arrive? Students offer reasons for and against, drawing on specific lines from Scene I. Teacher lists contrasting predictions on the board.

Teacher closes by asking: what one word best describes Mary at the end of Scene I? Students call out words; teacher notes 'confident', 'over-confident', 'eager'. This sharpens the dramatic irony before Scene II is read.

periods.teacher_notes: The table task at p.74 helps students see that Mrs. Shaw's instructions are very specific — she does not just say 'be polite' but models exact phrases. Students often miss that Mary's confidence ('I'm not a child!') is itself a signal of the trouble ahead. The prediction discussion works best if students commit to a position before Scene II is read.

periods.activity_title: Scene II: Every Blunder in Order

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (Scene II) — rectify five false statements about guest visit (p.77).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Scene II aloud (p.74–77) with students sharing the roles of Mrs. Shaw, Mary, Mrs. Harding, and Mrs. Lee in rotating small groups. Stage directions in brackets are read aloud as well, foregrounding the repeated 'No one speaks' silence.

Students work individually on the five 'rectify the false statement' items (p.77), correcting each sentence by returning to the play text. Teacher pauses on the 'Towzer' moment and the banker revelation to check that students track the connections.

Class reviews answers collaboratively. For each corrected statement teacher asks: which blunder in the play does this correspond to? Students identify the specific exchange, reinforcing sequence of events and narrative cause-and-effect.

periods.teacher_notes: Scene II is dense with comic reversals — each one hinges on Mary not knowing who she is talking about. Students frequently mix up Mrs. Lee's brother and Mr. Best; the banker confusion is a separate blunder from the newspapers one. The rectification exercise forces students to locate the exact exchange rather than guess from memory.

periods.activity_title: Thinking Deeper: Extracts, Silence and Character

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Extract 1: Mrs. Shaw's future-social-skills remark and Mary's traits (p.78).
Let us think and reflect — answer analytical questions on atmosphere, attitude change, and lesson of play (p.79).

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Extract 2: Mrs. Cotter questions (p.79): answer individually at home.

time_bands.activity: Students re-read Extract 1 (Mrs. Shaw on future social visits, p.78) and discuss in pairs: what exactly is Mrs. Shaw implying, and which trait — eager, inexperienced, or cautious — fits each character? Pairs then share conclusions with the class.

Teacher leads a class discussion on three analytical questions from p.79: what 'No one speaks' signals about atmosphere; how Mary's attitude shifts across the visit; and how the play argues for the value of polite conversation. Students note a key phrase for each answer.

Teacher wraps up by naming the comic technique: dramatic irony — the audience knows what Mary does not. Students suggest one moment where they felt this most sharply, and teacher records two or three on the board as a reference for future discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: The repeated stage direction 'No one speaks' is the play's sharpest comic device; students benefit from being shown how silence functions as dialogue. The 'attitude change' question (p.79) sometimes elicits vague responses — push students to cite the specific blunder where Mary first looks embarrassed rather than confident. Extract 2 (Mrs. Cotter section, p.79) is set as self-study homework because its four sub-questions are well within independent reach.

periods.activity_title: Listening for Manners: A Mother–Son Conversation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — fill-in-blank MCQs while listening to mother-son manners conversation (p.84).
Let us listen — second listen: select four true statements from seven (p.84).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the two fill-in-the-blank questions (p.84) aloud so students know what to listen for. Students write the question numbers in their notebooks, ready to note answers as the transcript is read.
Teacher reads the mother-son transcript (p.89) at a measured pace, pausing naturally at each new speaker. Students listen and select the correct option for each blank; no discussion yet.
Students read the seven statements for the second task (p.84) before the second reading. Teacher reads the transcript again. Students mark which four they judge to be true.

Class reviews both tasks together. For the true-statement task, teacher discusses why statements 4 and 5 are false, pointing to the exact lines in the transcript that contradict them. Students correct their work.

Teacher invites a brief response: one manner from the transcript that appears in the play as well. Students name the connection — for instance, the value of listening before speaking — before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript at p.89 uses informal domestic dialogue, so students comfortable with the play's register should follow it well. The key error in the seven-statements task is treating statement 6 ('receives all advice readily') as true — the son initially hesitates. Invite students who find listening tasks challenging to re-read the transcript silently after the oral readings.

periods.activity_title: Stress, Pitch and Meaning: Sounding Like Mary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak — falling intonation and word stress: four declarative sentences (p.85).
Let us speak — stress-shift activity: five versions of 'I didn't hurt anyone today', paired matching (p.85).

time_bands.activity: Teacher models falling intonation on 'I saw Mrs. Cotter this afternoon' (p.85), marking the pitch drop on the final syllable. Students repeat in chorus, then in pairs, with the teacher checking that the stress lands on 'Mrs. Cotter'.

Students practise the three additional declarative sentences from the play (p.85) with falling intonation and appropriate word stress, working in pairs. Teacher circulates and models corrected stress placement for common errors.

Pairs work through the five versions of 'I didn't hurt anyone today' (p.85), each stressing a different word and matching the spoken sentence to its meaning from the list. Each pair performs one version aloud for the class, who call out the matching meaning.

Teacher draws out the key insight: a single sentence can carry five different meanings depending on which word is stressed. Students note one takeaway about how stress affects meaning in conversation.

periods.teacher_notes: Stress-shift is genuinely novel for most students at this stage; the five-sentence matching activity is the most productive part of this unit. Students sometimes stress the wrong syllable within a word rather than the wrong word in the sentence — keep the focus on word-level emphasis, not syllable-level. The rising-intonation task (p.86) is left for self-study as it builds directly on the falling-intonation work just completed.

periods.activity_title: From Play to Story: Retelling Mary's Catastrophe

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — rewrite the play as a short story, using given hints, in class (p.86).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the writing task and hints aloud (p.86): introduce Mary and Mrs. Shaw, outline the coaching, narrate the guest visit, include humour and awkwardness, close on the inverted farewell. Class discusses briefly what makes a story different from a play script — narration, tense, descriptive language.

Students plan their story in four to five bullet points before writing: opening scene, Mrs. Shaw's instructions, the blunders in order, and the comic ending. Teacher asks two students to share their plan aloud to model the structure.

Students write their short story independently. Teacher circulates, prompting descriptive language at key comic moments — for example, the 'No one speaks' silences and Mary's growing panic — and checking that students use paragraphs.

Students exchange their draft with a partner for a quick peer read: the partner marks one moment that reads as genuinely funny and one sentence where the narration is unclear. Students note the feedback on their draft before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes reproduce the play's dialogue verbatim rather than converting it to reported speech and narrative; prompt them to use phrases like 'Mary announced confidently' and 'an uncomfortable silence fell'. The peer-response step is brief but keeps the draft alive without requiring revision time the unit does not have. The story is completed, peer-read and annotated — all within this unit.

periods.activity_title: Word-Building with Suffixes: Roots, Rules and Tenses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — divide words into root + suffix: gladly, banker, guidance, quietly, walking (p.80).
Let us learn — match suffixes to meanings and add examples in Column 4 (p.80).
Let us learn — fill blanks with suffixed forms of given root words (p.81).

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'humorous', 'hilariously', 'beautiful' on the board and invites students to strip the suffixes. Class derives the four suffixes (-ous, -ly, -ing, -ful), then applies this to the five words from the text: gladly, banker, guidance, quietly, walking (p.80).

Students complete the suffix-matching table (p.80): eight suffixes, eight meanings, plus one example each. Teacher draws attention to suffixes that change word class (noun to adjective, adjective to adverb) versus those that change form only (plural, past tense).

Students fill in the six blanks (p.81) by adding appropriate suffixes to the root words in brackets: effective → effectively, wise → wisely, discuss → discussion, respect → respectful, appreciate → appreciation, response → responsive. Class checks answers together.

Teacher closes with a rapid oral round: students name one word from the play that uses a suffix studied today and say which class it belongs to. This reinforces the connection between suffix knowledge and reading the play's vocabulary.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently treat 'guidance' as root 'guide' + suffix '-ance' without noticing the spelling change (drop 'e'). The suffix matching table (p.80) is the anchor task for this unit; the fill-in task (p.81) is a productive application of the same principle. Grammar tasks on confusable verb pairs (say/tell, see/look, etc.) and tense work (p.81–83) are left for self-study.

periods.activity_title: Tenses in Action and Stepping Beyond the Play

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — fill blanks: present continuous vs present perfect continuous in a play-organising context (p.82–83).
Let us explore — discuss how 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' connects to the play's theme of polite interaction (p.87).

homework.task_brief: Let us explore — research guest greetings in different languages and share with class (p.87).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reviews the two tense forms — simple past and present perfect continuous — using examples from the play: 'They lived in London before' versus 'She has been staying with them for a while' (p.82). Students then complete the seven blanks in the play-organising context passage (p.82–83), distinguishing ongoing actions from completed ones.

Teacher introduces the phrase 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' (p.87), its origin in the Maha Upanishad and its use at the G20 Summit. Small groups discuss the connection: if the world is one family, how should one speak to guests? Students draw two parallels with specific moments in the play.

Groups share one parallel each. Teacher notes recurring ideas on the board — empathy, listening, not embarrassing others — and links them back to Mrs. Shaw's core advice in Scene I. Students note one phrase from 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' that could serve as a subtitle for the play.

periods.teacher_notes: The present perfect continuous (has/have + been + -ing) causes consistent confusion at this stage — students default to simple present. Using the play's own example 'She has been staying with them' before moving to the gap-fill is effective scaffolding. The 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' discussion brings genuine cultural depth to the play's social comedy; encourage students to think beyond India-specific customs.

periods.activity_title: Synthesis: What Mary Taught Us About Conversation

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a quick whole-class game: students hear four statements about the play and call out whether each is spoken by Mary, Mrs. Shaw, Mrs. Harding, or Mrs. Lee. This warm-up activates recall of character voices, comedy of errors, and the inverted farewell at the play's close.

Class revisits the play's three biggest blunders — the 'beautiful children' opening, the Towzer dog episode, and the inverted goodbye — and analyses each through the lens of what conversational rule was broken. Students use vocabulary from the suffix and grammar work (respectful, responsive, appreciative) to name what Mary lacked.

Students write a short reflection (eight to ten sentences) in their exercise books from Mary's point of view, set the evening after the visit: what she now understands about polite conversation and what she would do differently. They draw on falling-intonation awareness, the manners conversation from the listening transcript, and the 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' idea of mutual respect.

Three or four students read their reflections aloud. Class identifies where each reflection captures dramatic irony — Mary knowing what she did not know before — and compares how different students imagined Mary's tone: remorseful, still over-confident, or genuinely changed. Teacher closes by naming the chapter's core insight: good conversation is an act of empathy, not a performance.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the play's content as taught across the chapter — the comic blunders, Mrs. Shaw's coaching rules, the mother-son manners dialogue, suffix and tense work, and the 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' theme — but each activity is self-contained: students need only their textbook and what they know of the play. The brief reflective writing is completed and shared within the unit; it does not continue any earlier draft.

items.item_stem: In Scene I of 'Say the Right Thing', Mrs. Shaw gives Mary a very specific instruction about what to say when guests prepare to leave. Which of the following best explains why Mrs. Shaw feels this instruction is necessary?

options.label: A
options.text: She believes Mrs. Harding and Mrs. Lee are likely to leave very early without warning.

options.label: B
options.text: She hopes Mary will take over as hostess so that she can attend to other household tasks.

options.label: C
options.text: She knows Mary tends to respond impulsively and may say something that embarrasses the family.

options.label: D
options.text: She wants Mary to practise formal English phrases used in polite society.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Students who choose this focus on the phrasing itself rather than on Mrs. Shaw's knowledge of Mary's character.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests students read the instruction as a practical social tip rather than a pre-emptive correction of Mary's impulsiveness.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Introduces a motivation not supported by anything Mrs. Shaw says or does in Scene I.

items.source_lo: Student interprets character motivation, dramatic irony, and the consequences of social misjudgement using dialogue as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Mary's serial blunders with guests Mrs. Harding and Mrs. Lee; Mrs. Shaw's coaching; 'No one speaks' stage direction; inverted farewell.
items.item_stem: Throughout Scene II of the play, the stage direction 'No one speaks' appears repeatedly after each of Mary's blunders. What does this recurring silence reveal about the dramatic technique the playwright uses, and how does it shape the audience's experience of the comedy?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The repeated 'No one speaks' direction signals that Mary's remarks have caused embarrassment to the guests without them responding directly. It creates dramatic irony — the audience understands the social damage being done even as Mary remains oblivious — and intensifies the humour by letting the silence speak louder than any reply.

items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between Rohan and his mother. According to the conversation, what does the mother say polite words like 'please' and 'thank you' show to other people?

options.label: B
options.text: That you are shy and prefer not to speak directly.

options.label: C
options.text: That you are well-educated and come from a good family.

options.label: D
options.text: That you want people to do things for you quickly.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Students who choose this import a social-class assumption not present in the transcript.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests a misreading of the mother's purpose — she explains the relational value of polite words, not their functional usefulness.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses politeness with shyness; the transcript explicitly links 'please' and 'thank you' to respect and gratitude.

items.source_context: Mother–son conversation on patience, polite words, apologising, inside voice, and queue behaviour (transcript p.89).
items.item_stem:
Listen to the mother-son conversation again. Decide whether each statement below is true or false, and give a brief reason drawn from the conversation.
1. The mother brings up the grocery queue incident to scold Rohan for bad behaviour.
2. Rohan understands that apologising shows he is responsible and did not intend to cause harm.
3. The mother tells Rohan that it is acceptable to speak loudly in a library as long as people nearby do not complain.

options.text: Rohan understands that apologising shows he is responsible and did not intend to cause harm.
The mother brings up the grocery queue incident to scold Rohan for bad behaviour.
The mother tells Rohan that it is acceptable to speak loudly in a library as long as people nearby do not complain.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — The mother uses the incident as a teaching opportunity about patience and fairness, not as a scolding.
2. True — Rohan says apologising shows 'I didn't mean to do it and that I care', and the mother confirms it shows responsibility.
3. False — The mother says they should use an 'inside voice' in the library so as not to bother others.

expected_elements: Pitch drops noticeably towards the end of both utterances.
Stressed word is louder and held slightly longer than others.
Partner correctly identifies the stressed word each time.

items.item_stem: Mary's famous final line in the play is 'Oh, must you stay? Can't you go?' Imagine you are playing Mary in a class enactment. Speak this line in two ways: first, as someone confused and flustered who does not realise her mistake; second, as someone who has just understood the error and is mortified. Explain to your classmates how you changed your stress and intonation between the two versions.

expected_elements: First version: faster, rising or level intonation suggesting confusion.
Second version: slower, falling intonation with a pause before 'go'.
Student names which word(s) carry stress in each version.
Explanation links intonation choice to Mary's emotional state.

items.item_stem:
The play uses both simple past and present perfect continuous tense. Read the two sentences below and answer the question that follows.
Sentence 1: 'They lived in London before.'
Sentence 2: 'She has been staying with them for a while.'
Explain in two or three sentences why the playwright uses the simple past for Sentence 1 and the present perfect continuous for Sentence 2. What difference in meaning does each tense create?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The simple past in Sentence 1 ('lived') tells us that living in London is a completed action with a clear end — they no longer live there. The present perfect continuous in Sentence 2 ('has been staying') tells us the action of staying started in the past and is still continuing at the time of speaking. The difference is between a finished event and an ongoing one.

items.item_stem: The phrase 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' means 'the world is one family'. In the play 'Say the Right Thing', Mrs. Shaw tells Mary that being kind in conversation is the most important thing when guests visit. Identify TWO specific moments in the play where Mary's words contradicted the spirit of 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ', and explain why each moment was a failure of the principle.

expected_elements: Two specific blunders from the play are named and described accurately.
Each blunder is linked to the idea of failing to treat guests as family.
Explanation uses language of empathy, respect, or mutual care.
Response is structured in two clear parts, one per moment.

items.item_stem: Design a short project to explore how the idea of 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakaṁ' is expressed through hospitality customs in two different regions of India or in two different countries. Your project should include: (a) a brief description of each custom, (b) a comparison of how each custom reflects the idea that guests deserve care and respect, and (c) a connection to at least one moment in 'Say the Right Thing' where Mrs. Shaw tries to instil similar values in Mary.

expected_elements: Two distinct hospitality customs described with specific detail.
Comparison identifies a shared value: guests as honoured family.
Connection to a named moment from the play is clearly explained.
Project is organised with the three parts (a), (b), (c) addressed.
